video.title: 20 BORING Businesses Almost Nobody Has Started (Every One Still Wide Open)

summary: The video presents 20 under-served, mostly asset-based business ideas, from leasing land and placing coin-operated machines to renting warehouse space and operating digital billboards. For each, the narrator gives a price or other hard number, why the opportunity may be overlooked, and a first question to ask a relevant person. The examples are largely US-focused and presented as researched opportunities rather than the narrator’s operating businesses. The central lesson is to check local demand and terms by asking the people who own, manage, or use the relevant assets.

speakers.name: Harry
speakers.description: Narrator for Harry's Stealth Wealth; the transcript says Harry called a local airfield manager.

ideas.name: Cell carrier ground leases
ideas.one_liner: Lease a corner of land to a cell carrier for a tower or related site.
ideas.business_model: Recurring ground lease.
ideas.customer: Cell carriers or tower operators seeking sites; the landowner supplies the parcel.
ideas.problem: Carriers and tower scouts need locations to address coverage gaps.
ideas.offer: A suitable parcel for cell infrastructure.

pricing.notes: The narrator gives three different ranges; suitability and lease terms are not described.

acquisition_channels.details: Submit parcel coordinates to a tower lease consultancy's landowner intake form; the narrator says tower scouts also map coverage gaps and mail landowners.

ideas.delivery: Make land available under lease for carrier infrastructure. Site construction, maintenance, and responsibilities are not described.
unit_economics_claims: National ground lease range: $500–$2,500 per month.
Industry database average: $900–$1,300 per month.
Mature multicarrier sites: $7,000–$8,000 per month.
tools: Tower lease consultancy landowner intake form

acquisition.how: An agent could prepare parcel details and submit an intake form; selecting a site and negotiating a lease need human review.

onboarding.how: An agent could collect parcel documents, but suitability, title, and lease terms need human review.

delivery.how: After a lease and site are agreed, land access is mostly passive; site issues still need an owner contact.

billing.how: Recurring invoices and payment reconciliation could be automated.

support.how: Agents could handle routine queries, but access, maintenance, and lease disputes need human oversight.

uk_applicability.notes: Ground leases can apply in the UK, but carrier demand, planning, access, and lease terms vary by site and local rules.

risks: A parcel may not suit a carrier's coverage or engineering needs.
Long-term access, planning, maintenance, and lease obligations need careful review.

quotes.text: National ground leases run roughly $500 to $2,500 a month with the industry database average sitting around 900 to$1,300.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Pipeline and utility easements
ideas.one_liner: Negotiate payment for a permanent easement across land.
ideas.business_model: One-off payment for an easement; no recurring model is stated.
ideas.customer: Pipeline or utility companies seeking rights across private land.
ideas.problem: Infrastructure providers need routes across land, while landowners may accept the first offer without negotiating.
ideas.offer: Permission to use a defined strip of land for utility or pipeline infrastructure.

pricing.model: Payment per rod or per acre for a permanent easement
pricing.notes: The narrator says regional rates exist in writing and that the first offer is negotiable.

acquisition_channels.details: Search the state's landowner easement guide and call a county extension office to ask what nearby easements paid.

ideas.delivery: Grant an easement after negotiating its terms. The transcript does not describe legal, survey, or construction work.
unit_economics_claims: Payments of $7–$40 per rod, stated as roughly $2,000–$4,200 per acre for a permanent easement.

acquisition.how: The stated research involves a call; negotiation and landowner decisions require human involvement.

onboarding.how: An agent could organize documents, but land boundaries and legal terms need human review.

delivery.how: Once granted, the right is largely documented and passive, subject to the agreed terms.

billing.how: A one-off payment can be tracked and reconciled by software, with a human checking the agreement.

support.how: Questions about access, damage, or easement scope need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Utility easements exist in the UK, but rights, compensation, and negotiation processes depend on the infrastructure and applicable law.

risks: The value and long-term effects depend on the land and easement terms.
A landowner should understand the rights granted before signing.

quotes.text: Payments run $7 to $40 per rod, which works out around $2,000 to $4,200 an acre for a permanent easement.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Mineral rights checks
ideas.one_liner: Check whether mineral rights remain attached to a property's surface deed.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; the idea is to investigate rights under land, not a described operating business.
ideas.customer: A landowner who may hold mineral rights.
ideas.problem: Owners may assume mineral rights were severed generations ago and never check.
ideas.offer: Determine whether mineral rights remain attached to the property.

price_points.label: Narrator says the check is free

pricing.notes: No revenue model or value of mineral rights is stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Call the county recorder and ask whether mineral rights remain attached to the surface deed.

ideas.delivery: Check public property records or commission a formal title search. No business delivery model is described.
unit_economics_claims: The narrator says a courthouse check is free and a formal title search costs $50–$150.

acquisition.how: The proposed first step is a phone call to a county recorder.

onboarding.how: An agent could gather parcel information, but identity, title, and rights need human verification.

delivery.how: Records may be searchable online, but formal title interpretation needs qualified human review.

billing.how: A title-search fee could be paid and recorded through standard software.

support.how: Questions about ownership and rights need human or professional advice.

uk_applicability.notes: Mineral rights and property records exist in the UK, but ownership and access procedures differ from US county records.

risks: The transcript gives no expected value or income from mineral rights.
A record check may not settle complex title questions.

quotes.text: A courthouse check is free and takes about 15 minutes. A formal title search runs $50 to $150.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Renting a boat slip
ideas.one_liner: Rent an available waterfront boat slip for a season.
ideas.business_model: Seasonal rental by boat length.
ideas.customer: Boat owners looking for a slip.
ideas.problem: Small lake towns may have too few slips, while waterfront owners may think renting one slip requires running a marina.
ideas.offer: Seasonal access to a boat slip.

price_points.label: One municipal marina rate; power included

pricing.notes: Insurance, liability, and paperwork vary; the narrator says a one-page seasonal agreement may be used.

acquisition_channels.details: Call a municipal marina to ask its per-foot rate and whether there is a waiting list.

ideas.delivery: Provide access to a slip for the season. The transcript does not describe maintenance or marina operations.
unit_economics_claims: Seasonal rates of $8–$88 per foot; a 30-foot boat is said to pay roughly $1,000–$7,000 per season.
One municipal marina publishes $75 per foot with power included.

acquisition.how: The stated first step is a call to a marina; arranging a private slip may also require direct contact.

onboarding.how: An agent could collect boat and renter details and prepare an agreement, with a human checking access and terms.

delivery.how: Access can be scheduled, but physical site upkeep and any marina services need human attention.

billing.how: Seasonal payment and reminders can be automated.

support.how: Routine booking questions can be automated; access and safety issues need a human.

uk_applicability.notes: Boat-slip rental also makes sense in the UK, though demand, marina rules, insurance, and local prices will differ.

risks: Waterfront access, safety, insurance, liability, and local rules may affect the offer.
Seasonal demand and slip suitability are location-dependent.

quotes.text: Seasonal rates run $8 to $88 per foot. So, a 30foot boat pays roughly $1,000 to $7,000 for one season.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Coin-operated kiddie rides
ideas.one_liner: Place coin-operated children's rides at grocery store entrances and split the cash with the store.
ideas.business_model: Pay-per-play machine revenue, with a store split implied but not quantified.
ideas.customer: Families shopping at local grocery stores; the store is the placement partner.
ideas.problem: A store may have unused entrance space and no local ride operator.
ideas.offer: A coin-operated ride outside a supermarket.

pricing.notes: The video says one machine grosses $600–$2,400 monthly before the store split; it does not state the operator's share.

acquisition_channels.details: Walk into one local grocery store and ask the store manager, not head office.

ideas.delivery: Own or operate a coin-operated ride placed at a store. The transcript does not describe maintenance or collections, which are physical tasks.
unit_economics_claims: At $1 per play and 20–80 plays a day, one machine is said to gross $600–$2,400 per month before the store split.

acquisition.how: Placement is obtained by asking a store manager in person.

onboarding.how: An agent could record the placement agreement, but installation and site approval need a person.

delivery.how: The machine takes payment automatically, but physical servicing, restocking, and collection need human visits.

billing.how: Cash accounting and partner splits can be recorded in software, but cash handling remains manual.

support.how: A broken or unsafe ride needs an in-person response.

uk_applicability.notes: Coin-operated children's rides can work in UK retail settings, subject to site permission, safety, and local requirements.

risks: The gross figure is before the store split and any operating costs.
Machine breakdowns, safety, cash collection, and store permission require attention.

quotes.text: The little horse outside the supermarket at a dollar a play and 20 to 80 plays a day. One machine grosses $600 to $2,400 a month before the stores split.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Coin-operated pool tables and dart boards
ideas.one_liner: Place coin-operated pool tables or dart boards in bars and split collections with the bar.
ideas.business_model: Revenue split with the bar; the cited standard is 50/50.
ideas.customer: Bar patrons; the bar owner is the placement partner.
ideas.problem: Bars may lack games that entertain customers and generate additional revenue.
ideas.offer: A coin-operated pool table or dart board, with no upfront cost to the bar in the proposed pitch.

pricing.notes: No earnings or dart-board cost is stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Walk into a bar that has no table and offer a 50/50 split with no upfront cost to the bar.

ideas.delivery: Place equipment in the bar and collect and split cash. The transcript describes a local, face-to-face placement model.
unit_economics_claims: A route company's published standard is a 50/50 split of cash collected.
A used pool table costs $1,200–$2,500.
ideas.startup_cost: A used pool table is stated to cost $1,200–$2,500; other setup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: The narrator says placement is face to face; in-person sales require a human.

onboarding.how: An agent could prepare a split agreement, but placement and bar approval need a person.

delivery.how: Tables and boards require physical installation, maintenance, and cash collection.

billing.how: A revenue split can be calculated in software, but cash collection and verification are manual.

support.how: Equipment faults and bar relationship issues need a human visit.

uk_applicability.notes: Bar game placements can work in the UK; venue permission, equipment rules, and commercial terms will vary.

risks: The 50/50 split and equipment cost do not establish likely earnings.
A local route needs physical maintenance, cash handling, and trusted accounting with venues.

quotes.text: Walk into one bar that has no table and offer the 50/50 with no upfront cost to them.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Digital jukebox placement
ideas.one_liner: Place app-driven digital jukeboxes in bars under a revenue-sharing agreement.
ideas.business_model: Revenue split between operator and bar, with licensing and wireless costs.
ideas.customer: Bar patrons; bars are the placement partners.
ideas.problem: Small-town bars may be overlooked by reps focused on larger city markets.
ideas.offer: An app-driven jukebox that plays customer-selected music.

pricing.notes: The transcript gives an example of a jukebox earning $600 per month; see metric claims.

acquisition_channels.details: Ask a local bar whether its jukebox is leased for a flat fee or runs on a revenue split.

ideas.delivery: Install and operate a digital jukebox in a bar; the transcript describes it as app-driven and notes licensing and wireless costs.
unit_economics_claims: On $600 monthly jukebox earnings, the bar gets $300 and the operator keeps roughly $180–$210 after licensing and a $30 wireless fee.

acquisition.how: The proposed first move is to ask a bar directly; placing equipment requires a human relationship.

onboarding.how: Account setup could be handled digitally, but placement and venue terms need approval.

delivery.how: Playback and payments may be app-driven, while installation, service, and licensing oversight remain.

billing.how: Digital transactions and recurring wireless charges could be reconciled automatically.

support.how: Agents could answer basic questions; broken equipment and licensing issues need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: The venue model is portable, but music licensing, platform availability, and commercial terms need UK-specific checking.

risks: The example is not a guaranteed outcome and is before unspecified costs.
Music licensing, connectivity, hardware service, and venue terms affect the economics.

quotes.text: A jukebox earning $600 a month hands the bar 300 and the operator keeps roughly 180 to 210 after licensing and a $30 wireless fee.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Coin-counting machines
ideas.one_liner: Supply coin-counting kiosks to regional grocery chains or credit unions.
ideas.business_model: Consumer fee per coin-counting transaction, with a share paid to the host store.
ideas.customer: Consumers needing coins counted; grocery chains and credit unions are host locations.
ideas.problem: Consumers need a way to turn coins into cash, and regional hosts may need a supplier.
ideas.offer: A self-service coin-counting machine placed in a host location.

pricing.model: Transaction fee with a host-store share
pricing.notes: The video says independent kiosks for regional chains and credit unions may be a different opportunity from the dominant national operator.

acquisition_channels.details: Call one regional grocery chain's operations office and ask who supplies its machine.

ideas.delivery: Install and maintain a coin-counting kiosk and share a portion of the consumer fee with the host. Physical servicing is implied by the machine model.
unit_economics_claims: The dominant national operator charges consumers 8.9%–12.9% and shares about 11.2% of that fee with the host store.

acquisition.how: The first move is a direct phone call to a chain's operations office.

onboarding.how: An agent could assemble a proposal, but host approval and machine installation require human involvement.

delivery.how: Transactions are self-service, but cash handling, servicing, and repairs are physical.

billing.how: Transaction fees and host shares could be calculated by software, with cash reconciliation checked by a person.

support.how: Cash jams, machine faults, and customer issues can require an in-person response.

uk_applicability.notes: Self-service coin counting could operate in UK retail or financial locations, subject to host demand and local payment rules.

risks: The cited fees describe a dominant operator, not a new entrant's margins.
Hardware, cash security, maintenance, and host contracts are not costed.

quotes.text: The dominant national operator charges consumers somewhere between 8.9 and 12.9% to turn coins into cash and shares about 11.2% of that fee with the host store.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Oxygen bar kiosk
ideas.one_liner: Place an oxygen bar station in a day spa on a revenue share.
ideas.business_model: Revenue share with a host spa; the current rate is not stated.
ideas.customer: Day-spa visitors; the spa is the proposed host.
ideas.problem: The narrator frames the idea as a forgotten fad whose equipment may still be available.
ideas.offer: An oxygen bar station hosted in a local day spa.

pricing.model: Revenue share; current pricing not stated.
pricing.notes: The narrator says there is no fresh national rate card.

acquisition_channels.details: Call one local day spa and ask whether it would host a station on a revenue share.

ideas.delivery: Provide a station for customers at a host spa. Equipment operation, maintenance, and safety procedures are not described.
unit_economics_claims: The narrator says oxygen bars ran about $1 per minute in the early 2000s; no current national rate is stated.

acquisition.how: The stated approach is a direct call to a local spa.

onboarding.how: An agent could document a host agreement, but equipment approval and placement need a person.

delivery.how: The kiosk may be self-service, but equipment, hygiene, and customer safety require physical oversight.

billing.how: A revenue share could be calculated digitally if transactions are recorded.

support.how: Equipment and customer issues require an on-site response.

uk_applicability.notes: A spa kiosk is physically possible in the UK, but the transcript gives no current demand or rate and health-related claims or safety requirements need checking.

risks: The pricing is historical and the narrator says no fresh national rate card is available.
The business may have weak demand as a forgotten fad; equipment and safety obligations are not described.

quotes.text: Back in the early 2000s, this ran about a dollar a minute, and since then, nobody has published a fresh national rate card.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Costume and mascot suit rental
ideas.one_liner: Rent mascot suits and ordinary adult costumes to schools, teams, and other local customers.
ideas.business_model: Daily costume rental.
ideas.customer: Schools, local sports teams, and people renting adult costumes.
ideas.problem: The category is often treated as Halloween-only, while schools and teams may need mascot suits year-round.
ideas.offer: Mascot suits and ordinary adult costumes for events, games, fundraisers, and open days.

pricing.notes: No cleaning, deposit, or delivery fees are stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Call a school athletics office and ask who currently supplies and maintains its mascot costume.

ideas.delivery: Rent costumes to customers and maintain them between rentals. Cleaning, storage, and handover are physical work.
unit_economics_claims: Mid-market mascot rentals are stated at $150–$400 per day; ordinary adult costumes at $40–$150 per day.

acquisition.how: The suggested first move is a direct call to a school athletics office.

onboarding.how: An agent could handle booking details and deposits, with a person checking fit and condition.

delivery.how: Physical handover, cleaning, repairs, and storage cap delivery automation.

billing.how: Bookings, deposits, invoices, and reminders can be automated.

support.how: Agents can answer booking questions, but sizing, damage, and late returns need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Schools, sports teams, and event rentals exist in the UK; local pricing, insurance, and customer demand need checking.

risks: Costumes need cleaning, repair, storage, and reliable return handling.
The cited rates are not tied to a location or utilization level.

quotes.text: Mid-market mascot rentals run $150 to $400 a day against 40 to 150 for ordinary adult costumes.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Wall advertising brokerage
ideas.one_liner: Secure a building wall and resell its advertising space to advertisers.
ideas.business_model: Lease wall space for a lower amount and resell advertising inventory.
ideas.customer: Advertisers seeking wall space; building owners supplying suitable walls.
ideas.problem: Owners may not think of a blank wall as an asset, and advertisers and property owners may not be connected.
ideas.offer: Broker access to a visible wall for an advertising campaign.

pricing.model: Resell advertising space while paying the owner a wall lease.

price_points.label: Big wall space in major metros
Wall lease described as a few hundred to a thousand

pricing.notes: The transcript does not give costs for production, permits, brokerage, or vacancy.

acquisition_channels.details: Identify a blank wall on a busy street, look up its owner in county property records, and ask whether anyone has offered money for it.

ideas.delivery: Arrange the wall lease and sell advertising cycles. Production, installation, and campaign management are not described.
unit_economics_claims: Big wall space is said to resell for $10,000–$50,000 per four-week cycle in major metros.
Midsize-market prices are said to range from $650–$14,000 per month.
The wall itself is leased for a few hundred to $1,000.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the narrator says the wall itself may be leased for a few hundred to a thousand.

acquisition.how: The first move is to identify an owner and ask directly; pitching property owners and advertisers needs human sales.

onboarding.how: Agents could collect campaign specifications, but wall rights and creative approvals need human review.

delivery.how: Physical advertising installation and maintenance require people.

billing.how: Campaign invoices and recurring cycle reminders could be automated.

support.how: Routine campaign updates can be automated; property and installation issues need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Outdoor advertising brokerage can work in the UK, but planning, advertising rules, property rights, and market rates differ.

risks: Property permission, planning, advertising rules, and installation costs are not covered.
A broker needs both a suitable wall and an advertiser; a vacant cycle can erase the expected margin.

quotes.text: Big wall space resells for $10,000 to $50,000 per 4-week cycle in major metros and even midsize markets publish 650 to 14,000 a month.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Medical and mobility equipment rental
ideas.one_liner: Offer same-day cash-pay rentals of mobility equipment such as knee scooters and wheelchairs.
ideas.business_model: Short-term equipment rental by the week.
ideas.customer: Post-surgical patients and others needing temporary mobility equipment.
ideas.problem: Patients may need equipment today for a short recovery, while local suppliers may focus on insurance billing.
ideas.offer: Knee scooters and wheelchairs for short-term rental.

price_points.label: Wheelchair rate range as transcribed; rate card period is not specified

pricing.notes: The transcript says '$50 to $1 175 across several published rate cards'; it does not clarify whether the wheelchair range is weekly.

acquisition_channels.details: Call an orthopedic office and ask what it tells a patient who needs a knee scooter that afternoon.

ideas.delivery: Provide mobility equipment to patients, potentially same day. Delivery, cleaning, fitting, and collection are physical tasks.
unit_economics_claims: Knee scooters are stated at $25–$75 per week.
Wheelchair rate cards are transcribed as $50–$1,175, with the unit period unclear.

acquisition.how: The proposed first step is a direct call to an orthopedic office.

onboarding.how: An agent could collect booking and payment details; suitability and fitting need human oversight.

delivery.how: Equipment preparation, physical delivery, fitting, cleaning, and collection require people.

billing.how: Rental charges, deposits, and reminders can be automated.

support.how: A patient may need prompt human help with equipment faults or fit.

uk_applicability.notes: Short-term mobility rental can fit UK patient needs, but medical-device requirements, clinical referrals, delivery logistics, and prices need local checking.

risks: The transcript's wheelchair price range and rental period are unclear.
Hygiene, equipment condition, fit, safety, same-day delivery, and liability need careful handling.

quotes.text: Knee scooters go for $25 to $75 a week and wheelchairs for $50 to $1 175 across several published rate cards.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Prop house
ideas.one_liner: Rent furniture and set dressing to film and television productions in cities without local prop houses.
ideas.business_model: Rental of props and set dressing to productions.
ideas.customer: Film and television productions, including local production coordinators.
ideas.problem: Productions in newer locations may lack nearby prop houses and may truck furniture from elsewhere.
ideas.offer: A local inventory of props, furniture, and set dressing for productions.

pricing.model: Rental; rate basis is not stated.

price_points.label: Rentals implied by the stated budget share

pricing.notes: The figures are a broad budget share example, not a quoted price list for a new prop house.

acquisition_channels.details: Pull the state film commission's list of recent local productions and ask a coordinator where they rent from.

ideas.delivery: Maintain and rent props and furniture to productions. Inventory handling and transport are physical; the transcript does not describe operations in detail.
unit_economics_claims: Props and set dressing are said to run 4%–8% of production budgets.
For a $30 million series, the narrator calculates $1.2–$2.4 million of rented furniture.

acquisition.how: The first move is to find recent productions and contact a coordinator; production sales are relationship-based.

onboarding.how: Agents could handle inventory lists and bookings, with people confirming availability and production requirements.

delivery.how: Props and furniture need physical storage, handling, and transport.

billing.how: Quotes, rental periods, invoices, and reminders can be managed in software.

support.how: Changes, missing items, damage, and production deadlines need human response.

uk_applicability.notes: Film and television production rental can work in UK production locations, but local production volume, tax incentives, logistics, and inventory demand differ.

risks: The budget share does not establish the revenue a local entrant can capture.
Inventory investment, storage, transport, damage, and production scheduling are not costed.

quotes.text: Props and set dressing run 4 to 8% of a production's budget. On a $30 million series, that is 1.2 to$2.4 million of rented furniture.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: U-pick lavender field
ideas.one_liner: Run a lavender field with visitor picking, bundles, and oil sales.
ideas.business_model: Visitor admission or picking fees and sales by weight; bundles and oil are also mentioned.
ideas.customer: Visitors who want a farm experience and buyers of lavender products.
ideas.problem: The crop takes years to mature, discouraging operators who expect a fast return.
ideas.offer: A lavender field for visitors to pick, plus bundles and oil.

pricing.model: Per visitor or per pound, with product sales also mentioned.

price_points.label: Established field across bundles and oil

pricing.notes: The narrator gives a weekend gross example of $2,000–$7,000 with 100–200 visitors; crop maturity takes 2–3 years.

acquisition_channels.details: Consult the state extension office's specialty-crop guide for the local climate zone.

ideas.delivery: Grow lavender, host visitors for picking, and sell bundles and oil. Farming, visitor access, and harvest are physical operations.
unit_economics_claims: Published farm rates are $20–$35 per person or $15–$25 per pound.
A weekend with 100–200 visitors is said to gross $2,000–$7,000.
An established field can do $10,000–$30,000 per acre per year across bundles and oil.
Lavender takes 2–3 years to reach full bloom.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: The narrator says lavender takes 2–3 years to reach full bloom; time to first revenue is not stated.

acquisition.how: Agents could manage content, listings, and booking, while local visitor partnerships and promotion need human work.

onboarding.how: Visitor bookings and payment can be handled online with automated confirmations.

delivery.how: Farming, harvesting, visitor safety, and on-site experience require people.

billing.how: Online ticketing and product orders can be charged and reconciled automatically.

support.how: Weather, access, crop condition, and visitor issues need human oversight.

uk_applicability.notes: Lavender farms and visitor picking can work in parts of the UK, but climate, growing conditions, seasonality, land use, and visitor demand need local assessment.

risks: The crop takes years to mature, tying up land and capital before full bloom.
Weather, crop health, visitor safety, and seasonal demand affect results.

quotes.text: Lavender takes 2 to three years to reach full bloom. Everyone chasing a fast return quits before the plant matures.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Shipping container conversion
ideas.one_liner: Convert shipping containers into offices and sell or rent the finished units.
ideas.business_model: One-off sale or monthly rental of modified containers.
ideas.customer: Customers seeking a container office; the transcript does not specify a buyer segment.
ideas.problem: Container resellers and construction contractors may not connect container supply with finish-out work.
ideas.offer: A finished 20-foot container office or a modified container for rent.

pricing.notes: No conversion, transport, site, or maintenance costs are stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Call a container depot and ask who does local conversion work and whether it would refer customers.

ideas.delivery: Source a container, finish it as an office, then sell or rent it. Construction and transport are physical work.
unit_economics_claims: A finished 20-foot container office sells for $14,000–$22,000.
A modified container rents for $450–$850 per month.

acquisition.how: The first move is a direct call to a container depot; partnership development requires a person.

onboarding.how: Agents could collect specifications and arrange quotes, but site and build requirements need human review.

delivery.how: Container conversion, installation, and transport are physical tasks.

billing.how: Invoices and rental collections can be automated, with project costs checked by a person.

support.how: Build defects, delivery issues, and site problems require human response.

uk_applicability.notes: Container offices can be sold or rented in the UK, but planning, building standards, transport, and site requirements need local checking.

risks: Conversion, transport, and site preparation costs are not stated.
Planning and building requirements may affect whether a unit can be used as intended.

quotes.text: A finished 20ft container office sells for 14 to $22,000 and renting a modified one runs $450 to $850 a month.
quotes.speaker: Harry

ideas.name: Record storage warehouse
ideas.one_liner: Store and retrieve business records for local firms in a small warehouse.
ideas.business_model: Per-box-per-month storage, with retrieval fees also mentioned but not priced.
ideas.customer: Law firms, clinics, and accountants.
ideas.problem: Local firms need long-term records storage and may dislike retrieval fees; the middle ground between national logistics and personal storage may be underserved.
ideas.offer: Record storage with local retrieval service.

pricing.model: Per box per month; an archive also publishes a cubic-foot price.
pricing.notes: Retrieval fees are mentioned but not quantified.

acquisition_channels.details: Call a law firm's office manager and ask what it pays per box and whether a retrieval invoice has surprised it.

ideas.delivery: Store boxes in a warehouse and retrieve them when requested. The transcript says a small warehouse and racking are needed before the first box; handling and retrieval are physical.
unit_economics_claims: Independent per-box pricing is stated at $0.50–$0.95 per box per month.

warnings.warning: The narrator says the video is educational, not financial advice, and tells viewers to check local rules because zoning and permits vary.
The oxygen-bar price is historical: the narrator says it ran about $1 per minute in the early 2000s and that no fresh national rate card has been published.
The wine-storage case-rate wording is unclear in the transcript ('$310 to$10'); do not treat it as a reliable range.
The wheelchair rental range is transcribed as '$50 to $1 175' and the period is not stated.
The container-farm lease phrase 'while still open' is unclear; the stated $3,000 monthly amount needs verification.
The lavender example says the crop takes 2–3 years to reach full bloom, so a fast return should not be assumed.
The narrator says to find the escalation clause before signing a multi-year lease; without an annual increase, a stated $1,000 monthly rent remains $1,000 in 20 years.
The 20 opportunities are presented as a researched list, not as the narrator's own operating businesses; the video does not provide full startup costs, utilization, or net margins.
Physical businesses in the list require site permission and may involve safety, maintenance, insurance, transport, or local regulatory obligations not detailed in the video.

lessons.lesson: Test opportunities by asking the specific owner, manager, or customer what they currently do and what it costs before buying equipment or signing a lease.
